question: Does raising the minimum wage reduce employment? Weigh the Card and Krueger tradition against Neumark and Wascher, address the publication-bias literature on this question specifically, and state what the current best estimate of the employment elasticity is.

coverage.note: We know NW vs Card-Katz-Krueger was a dispute, but lack the actual empirical content: CK's original finding (no disemployment/small positive), NW's specific payroll-data critique, and how later reanalysis (e.g., Card-Krueger 2000 AER reply using BLS payroll data) resolved it.
No funnel-plot, PET-PEESE, or p-curve analyses (e.g., Doucouliagos-Stanley 2009, Card et al. meta-analyses) have been retrieved yet.
No data gathered on Cengiz et al. 2019, Dube-Lester-Reich, or Cengiz-Dube-Lindner-Zipperer bunching-estimator findings.
No evidence on minimum-wage 'bite' heterogeneity, Seattle $15 study, or California statewide low-wage-region effects gathered yet.
No sources address bidirectional publication bias or funding-source-driven suppression on either side.
No steelman case or NW rebuttal to bias-corrected near-zero estimates has been retrieved.
No CBO reports or other institutional elasticity ranges/estimates have been gathered.
No subgroup (teens vs. all low-wage workers) or industry-specific (restaurant) breakdown evidence gathered.

contradictions: No direct contradictions exist among the three confirmed claims, since they are narrow provenance statements; however, the confirmed evidence base contradicts the implicit expectation (from the coverage checklist and hypotheses) that this run would contain substantive empirical findings - it does not.

A claim asserting Neumark-Wascher's work had been cited 96 times was explicitly refuted/killed by the citation-support audit, illustrating that not all surface-plausible bibliometric claims in this space held up.

scopeContract.decisionAtStake: The reader is likely a policymaker, analyst, or informed commentator deciding how much weight to give disemployment-effect arguments when evaluating a proposed minimum wage increase (e.g., whether to support/oppose a hike, or how large an increase is 'safe'). If the answer is 'effects are negligible/near zero,' the reader may discount job-loss objections; if 'effects are real and sizeable for some groups,' the reader may favor smaller increases, phase-ins, or targeted alternatives (EITC) instead. Absent a specific pending decision, the deliverable functions as a calibrated literature synthesis to inform that class of decisions.
scopeContract.keyQuestion: Based on the accumulated quasi-experimental and meta-analytic evidence including corrections for publication bias, does raising the minimum wage cause a statistically and economically meaningful reduction in employment among low-wage/teen workers, and if so, what is the best current point estimate of that employment elasticity?
assumptions: Geographic scope is primarily the United States, since Card & Krueger and Neumark & Wascher both center on US state/local minimum wage variation; will note whether international evidence (UK, Germany, developing countries) generalizes or diverges.

Time horizon covers the empirical literature from the early 1990s (Card-Krueger 1994 NJ/PA study) through the most recent meta-analyses and monopsony-based studies (2020s), since publication-bias critiques and modern estimates (e.g., Cengiz et al. 2019, Card & Krueger, Neumark & Wascher's later syntheses) postdate the original debate.

'Employment elasticity' refers to the standard labor-demand elasticity concept: percentage change in employment (typically teen or low-wage/low-skill worker employment, or restaurant-sector employment) per 1% change in the minimum wage, not aggregate employment or GDP effects.

'Reduce employment' is treated as a question of the sign and magnitude of disemployment effects for the directly affected (low-wage/teen) population, not broader macroeconomic effects like inflation, small business closures, or automation substitution, unless the literature ties those explicitly to employment elasticity estimates.

'Serious' or 'meaningful' disemployment effect is assumed to mean an elasticity magnitude that is statistically distinguishable from zero and economically non-trivial (e.g., beyond roughly -0.1 to -0.3), a threshold not specified by the asker but commonly used in this literature to distinguish 'small/negligible' from 'substantial' effects.

The question is treated as an academic/empirical synthesis request rather than tied to a specific pending policy vote or minimum wage level, since no specific jurisdiction, wage level, or policy proposal was named.
whatWouldChangeTheAnswer: If publication-bias-corrected meta-analyses (e.g., Card & Krueger 1995's own meta-analysis, or more recent ones like Wolfson & Belman 2019, Neumark & Shirley 2022) converge on an elasticity indistinguishable from zero after correction, that would support the 'negligible effect' conclusion; if instead correction reveals bias in the OPPOSITE direction (i.e., true effects are more negative than published estimates suggest), that would flip toward 'real and larger than commonly cited.'

If recent high-powered quasi-experimental designs using modern synthetic control / border-discontinuity methods (e.g., Cengiz et al. 2019, Dube-Lester-Reich border county studies) find consistent near-zero effects even at higher minimum wage levels (e.g., $15 in Seattle/California), that strengthens the Card-Krueger tradition; if newer studies at higher minimum-wage-to-median-wage ratios (bite) show emerging disemployment effects not visible at lower historical minimum wages, that would flip the answer toward 'effects depend on bite/level' rather than a flat 'no effect.'

If Neumark & Wascher's critiques of Card-Krueger's data/methodology (e.g., payroll vs. survey data issues in the NJ-PA study) are found to be decisively vindicated or decisively refuted by independent replications (e.g., Card & Krueger's 2000 payroll-data reanalysis), that shifts credibility weight between the two camps.

If the elasticity varies substantially and systematically by subgroup (teens vs. all low-wage workers), by wage level relative to local median ('bite'), or by whether the local labor market is monopsonistic, a single 'best estimate' answer would need to be replaced with a conditional answer, changing the nature of the conclusion from a point estimate to a range/interaction effect.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The Card-Krueger view is largely correct: modern minimum wage increases (within observed historical ranges) have employment effects on low-wage/teen workers that are statistically indistinguishable from zero or very small (elasticity near 0 to -0.1), consistent with monopsony power or search frictions in low-wage labor markets.
hypotheses.killCriterion: Eliminated if publication-bias-corrected meta-analyses and modern high-powered studies (post-2015) consistently show statistically significant negative elasticities in the -0.2 to -0.4 range or larger, robust to bias correction, particularly for teens or low-wage workers at higher minimum-wage 'bite' levels.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The Neumark-Wascher view is largely correct: minimum wage increases produce real, economically meaningful disemployment effects for low-wage/teen workers, with elasticities commonly cited in the -0.1 to -0.3 range in the broader (non-cherry-picked) literature, and Card-Krueger-style null results reflect specific methodological limitations (small samples, short time horizons, offsetting margins like hours/turnover) rather than the true underlying relationship.
hypotheses.killCriterion: Eliminated if publication-bias-corrected meta-analyses (which explicitly test for and adjust away the file-drawer/p-hacking problem Neumark-Wascher's own survey-based tallies are accused of) show that the population of studies, once corrected, centers on a near-zero elasticity, or if Neumark & Wascher's own later work (e.g., Neumark & Shirley 2022) concedes convergence toward smaller effects than their earlier reviews claimed.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The true answer is conditional/heterogeneous rather than a single sign: employment effects are near zero for moderate minimum wages (low 'bite' relative to local median wage) but become negative and economically meaningful once the minimum wage crosses a higher bite threshold (e.g., >50-60% of local median wage), reconciling both literatures as looking at different policy regimes/time periods.
hypotheses.killCriterion: Eliminated if studies of high-bite minimum wages (e.g., Seattle's $15, California's statewide increases relative to low-wage regions) show no detectable disemployment effect even at high bite, or conversely if low-bite historical increases (the original Card-Krueger NJ case) are shown via reanalysis to have produced real job losses, undermining the threshold/bite explanation.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Publication bias is severe enough on BOTH sides (advocacy-funded studies from pro- and anti-minimum-wage-increase interests) that the literature cannot currently support a precise consensus point estimate; the honest 'best estimate' is a wide, low-confidence range (e.g., -0.05 to -0.2) rather than a specific number, and further methodological consensus (not just more studies) is needed.
hypotheses.killCriterion: Eliminated if a small number of well-identified, pre-registered or administrative-data-based studies (less susceptible to publication bias, e.g., using universal administrative payroll data across many states/countries) converge tightly on a specific elasticity value with narrow confidence intervals, indicating the field has effectively resolved the estimate despite bias in the broader literature.

summary: This synthesis run produced only three confirmed claims, all of which are provenance/metadata facts about the Card-Krueger vs. Neumark-Wascher dispute (who wrote what reply to whom, and when a review paper was published) rather than any empirical finding about employment effects. No claim in this run reports an actual elasticity estimate, a publication-bias-correction result (funnel plot, PET-PEESE, p-curve), or findings from modern post-2015 quasi-experimental studies. As a result, the user's core question - whether minimum wage increases reduce employment, and what the current best elasticity estimate is - cannot be answered from the evidence gathered; all four pre-registered hypotheses are marked untested. This should be treated as an incomplete research run requiring further evidence-gathering, not as a substantive finding of ambiguity in the literature itself.
answerFirst: The confirmed evidence in this run does NOT let us answer the substantive question of whether minimum wage increases reduce employment or what the current best elasticity estimate is. The only claims that survived adjudication establish provenance and timeline facts (that Neumark-Wascher directly disputed Card-Krueger-Katz starting in the early 1990s, and that Neumark-Wascher published a 2006 review paper) — none of the confirmed claims report an actual employment-effect finding, elasticity number, or publication-bias correction result. All four pre-registered hypotheses are therefore UNTESTED, not surviving or killed, because no confirmed claim contains the empirical content needed to adjudicate them. This report should be read as a coverage failure, not a null result.

hypothesisVerdicts.hypothesis: H2: Neumark-Wascher view largely correct - real disemployment effects, elasticities -0.1 to -0.3.
hypothesisVerdicts.killCriterion: Would be eliminated if bias-corrected meta-analyses showed the corrected population centers on near-zero elasticity, or if Neumark-Wascher's own reviewed studies were shown to suffer selective reporting; no such evidence was retrieved.
hypothesisVerdicts.reasoning: No confirmed claim contains Neumark-Wascher's or anyone else's actual elasticity estimates or a publication-bias-corrected reassessment of their survey-based tallies. Confirmed claims only establish authorship and timing of their papers.

hypothesisVerdicts.hypothesis: H3: Effect is conditional on minimum-wage 'bite' - near zero at low bite, negative at high bite (e.g., Seattle $15).
hypothesisVerdicts.killCriterion: Would be eliminated if high-bite studies showed no detectable disemployment effect, or if low-bite historical cases showed effects via reanalysis; no such evidence was retrieved either way.
hypothesisVerdicts.reasoning: No confirmed claim addresses minimum-wage bite, Seattle's $15 minimum, California statewide effects, or any heterogeneity analysis whatsoever.

hypothesisVerdicts.hypothesis: H4: Publication bias is severe on both sides; honest best estimate is a wide, low-confidence range (e.g., -0.05 to -0.2).
hypothesisVerdicts.killCriterion: Would be eliminated if a small number of well-identified administrative-data studies converged tightly on a specific elasticity; no such evidence was retrieved.
hypothesisVerdicts.reasoning: No confirmed claim addresses publication bias direction, severity, or administrative-data-based studies converging (or not) on a tight estimate. The only bias-adjacent item in this run was a citation-count claim that was refuted, which is unrelated to publication bias in the statistical sense.

strongestArgumentAgainst: One could argue the confirmed claims are still meaningful: they establish that a real, sustained, adversarial empirical dispute exists between two well-known camps (Card-Krueger-Katz vs. Neumark-Wascher) spanning at least 1993–2006, which is itself relevant context for the user's request to 'weigh' the two traditions. A synthesis could lean on general knowledge of this literature (e.g., that meta-analyses often report elasticities clustering near -0.1 to 0, with disagreement over publication bias direction) to give a substantive answer. However, doing so would inject unconfirmed facts not present in the adjudicated claims, violating the instruction not to add facts absent from the evidence above — so the honest position is that this run's evidence base is simply too thin to answer the empirical question, and any elasticity number offered here would be fabricated relative to the sourced claims.

caveats: This report cannot answer the user's actual question. All three confirmed claims are provenance/metadata facts (who wrote what, when) about the Card-Krueger vs. Neumark-Wascher dispute — none report an empirical finding, employment elasticity, or effect direction. The coverage checklist shows eight sub-questions unanswered or only partially answered, including: (1) the actual empirical content of Card-Krueger (1994) and Neumark-Wascher's (2000) payroll-data critique; (2) any publication-bias correction analysis (funnel plots, PET-PEESE, p-curve) specific to minimum-wage employment studies; (3) any post-2015 quasi-experimental studies (Cengiz et al. 2019, Dube-Lester-Reich, Seattle $15 study); (4) heterogeneity by minimum-wage 'bite'; (5) bidirectional publication bias; (6) the Neumark-Wascher steelman case; (7) institutional syntheses (e.g., CBO) with point estimates; (8) subgroup/industry breakdowns. A citation-count claim (96 citations) was explicitly refuted/killed and is reported here for transparency only. No T5 sources were used; no findings rest solely on T4 aggregators. Because the underlying empirical literature has moved substantially since 2006 (the one dated source in this run), any answer built only on these claims would be badly stale even if it existed.

honestLimits.partialCitationsAreKept: A `partial` citation verdict means the page points this way but the statement adds scope, certainty or specificity the page does not carry - and it does NOT remove the claim.
